papers.title: Effectiveness of a mindfulness-based cognitive behavioral program on glycemic control and quality of life among adults with diabetes in Damascus, Syria: a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: AIMS: Depression and diabetes distress worsen glycemic control and quality of life (QoL). This randomized controlled trial evaluated a 14-week mindfulness-based cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) program on Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) and QoL among adults with diabetes in Damascus, Syria. METHODS: Adults with diabetes and mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms were randomized to mindfulness-based CBT or routine care. Per-protocol analysis included 40 completers (n = 20/group). Post-intervention HbA1c was evaluated using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) adjusting for baseline levels. Secondary QoL was assessed across four WHOQOL-BREF domains. RESULTS: Intervention participants achieved significant reduction in HbA1c levels (9.0 ± 1.7% to 7.2 ± 1.4%, p = 0.021), while controls experienced an increase in HbA1c levels (9.1 ± 1.8% to 9.9 ± 1.7%, p < 0.001). ANCOVA demonstrated a significant intervention effect (F (1,37) = 13.53, p < 0.001, partial η CONCLUSIONS: Mindfulness-based CBT produced clinically meaningful glycemic and QoL improvements, supporting psychosocial care integration into routine diabetes management in crisis-affected settings. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07779044.

papers.title: 'The music pulls me through' - patient experiences of video-based group music therapy during cancer treatment: a qualitative study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Cancer patients undergoing active tumor therapy experience emotional strain and social isolation, while treatment-related side effects, immunosuppression, infection risk, and reduced mobility may limit access to psychosocial support. Although music therapy is an established component of supportive oncology care, evidence on video-based group music therapy remains limited, regarding therapeutic alliance, group cohesion, and patients' experiences. This study explored participants' experiences with a video-based online group music therapy intervention during cancer treatment. METHODS: This qualitative study examined experiences with a video-based online music therapy group intervention for adults undergoing cancer treatment. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 13 participants who completed eight weekly group sessions. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis following Mayring and reported in accordance with the COREQ criteria. RESULTS: Analysis yielded five categories: (1) expectations and initial attitudes, (2) perceived effects and evaluation of the intervention, (3) therapeutic alliance and group cohesion, (4) experiences with the online format, and (5) anticipated longer-term effects. Participants reported that music facilitated emotional awareness, reflection, and interpersonal exchange. Therapeutic alliance and group cohesion were described as developing over the course of the intervention despite the online setting. The online format improved accessibility by overcoming geographical barriers and reducing physical demands, while reduced in-person interaction, technical issues, and limited program duration were experienced as constraints. Participants described intentions to continue using music- and mindfulness-based strategies in everyday life. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that therapeutic alliance, group cohesion, and relational processes can develop in video-based online group music therapy. Intervention structure, facilitation, and duration appear to play a central role in shaping participants' experiences. Video-based music therapy groups may provide a feasible psycho-oncological support option for patients who face barriers to in-person participation. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The overarching intervention study was prospectively registered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00032339; registered 3 August 2023).

papers.title: Parenting Children With Externalizing Disorders: A Qualitative Study From South India.
papers.abstract: AimsExternalizing disorders are one of the most prevalent childhood disorders. This study aimed to understand the experiences of parents of children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD), and Conduct Disorder (CD) in the Indian context, with an equal representation of both fathers and mothers.MethodA qualitative exploratory design was utilized. 6 mothers and 5 fathers of children diagnosed with either ADHD, ODD, or CD were recruited using purposive sampling from the Department of Paediatrics and the Department of Clinical Psychology of a private hospital in India. The interviews followed a semi-structured schedule and were analyzed using thematic analysis.ResultsSix main themes were identified: child's behavior and emotional responsiveness, parental strain, imbalanced roles in the parental dyad, societal perceptions, reflective coping in parents, and parental concerns for the future. Parenting children with externalizing disorders was reported to be challenging, with most mothers facing an unequal burden. Children's need for screentime was an emerging concern.ImplicationsThe study implies the significant need to adapt interventions for Indian parents, keeping in mind cultural beliefs, while also ensuring adequate involvement of fathers in the treatment process. Regulation of screentime could be an additional target of intervention.
